We are bound by accommodating those we take as lovers,
no matter what shape they bring.
And we are hurt by rejection,
however it may appear.

Everyone carries a pain that resists the boxes of the DSM.
Everyone knows the gap between life and an excuse.
The idiosyncrasy is not exile.
It is membership in the human race.

But listen—don’t.
The part of you that never fits,
the spillover, the refusal—
that is not failure.
That is where we connect.
Don’t throw the very socket to the sea.

Play the part or be demoted.
In this day and age only named sufferings are heroic.
You are not special.
Surely you understand.
Surely you too demand a diagnosis
in exchange for love.

The name becomes armor,
and sorrow,
and shell.
You are no longer seen.
Only the label is visible.
Only the war is winning.

The war for empathy welcomes you, recruit.
You must carry your diagnosis at all times.
You must throw it forward whenever duty calls.
Make them understand you for the greater good.

You hesitate.
You glimpse the future.
And then it is done.
You found a way to fit in.

The deal is clear.
Without the name you are strange and dangerous.
With it you are legible and safe.
The name unlocks an accommodation,
but only for the part of you covered by the name.

Smiles and arms already open for an embrace.
Just say the name.
What are you?
How can you be understood?

But in shadow lurks the silent recognition:
your particular pain remains at least a bit unexplained.
It spills over edges,
leaves cavities to rust.
It refuses the name.
Your truth is adjacent,
always in training for the full thing.
potential allies in the struggle for empathy.

Depression. ADHD. Bipolar. PTSD. Autism. Take a pick.
A label above the head that fits its shape.
A hat with miraculous machinery that explains a thing,
connects with others of a similar affliction.

The deepest thing is also the simplest:
We can belong.
We remember how it feels.
We just need to keep finding our way back.

Now. Come. Sit.
This isn’t a movement. It isn’t a system. It’s a way of remembering who we are. And the remembering happens not in words, but in the small courage of knocking, of calling, of saying now?

At the core: life wants to be shared. The fire wants people around it. The soup wants to be ladled into more than one bowl. The story wants ears. The song wants a voice to carry it. The silence wants company.
something alive, something unpolished.

Spontaneity isn’t reckless. It’s trust. Trust that showing up half-formed is still enough. Trust that the world will meet us halfway if we give it the chance. Trust that the people around us are hungry for the same thing we are: something real,
sang together because it was the default. We have to choose it now. That’s harder, but it’s also more beautiful, because every choice is an act of love.

The deeper truth: loneliness is not natural. It’s a side effect of walls too thick, schedules too full, pride too heavy. Our ancestors weren’t saints—they just didn’t have the option of being alone all the time. They bumped into each other, ate together,

And the thing is, it doesn’t take much. A cup of tea. A hand of cards. Folding laundry while someone else keeps you company. It’s not about grand gestures. It’s about weaving the fabric back together in tiny threads.

Spontaneity matters because life doesn’t wait. The fine weather doesn’t last forever. The good mood, the joke, the song, the story that wanted to be told—they pass if we don’t catch them. Gathering in the moment is how we grab a piece of life before it slips.
We gather because it feels good. That’s it. That’s the whole thing. Not philosophy, not ritual. Just the truth of how humans are built.

This is a space for ease and curiosity. Who knows what the morning will bring? It fully depends on who shows up and what do they want, really want. Let the gathring be defined by an expectation for surprise.

Now. Come. Sit.
It doesn’t need to be more complicated than that. The point is to show up, to be present, to remember that connection doesn’t always need so much planning.

You don't want to be the leader who finds out a year later that a guy you had a bad feeling about assaulted some girl, & deep down you knew it would happen sometime, but you didn't want to appear too harsh. Take the blow to your reputation, if your intuition is strong.
One of the hardest (good) calls to make as a sheepdog is a harsh call that will really affect someone's life, but is based on intuition--but these are often the most important ones to make

3) When making calls based on intuition, sheepdogs should be aware of the pitfalls both of projecting her personal baggage unfairly, *and* of gaslighting herself when she can't name explicit reasons, but *know* something is off.

2) should always distinguish personal issues from community issues (*you* may have been harmed by the guy, but if he doesn't seem to be a threat to anyone else as a pattern, keep it between the two of you. Don't be a bully.)

All this said, sheepdogs should 
1) set boundaries in proportion to their perception of the harms (while balancing awareness of community resources),

Your community is not so special as to be the only place in the modern world where this person can gain the skills to be a functional, positive contributor to a community. We must have more faith than that. Sometimes wolves don't believe in themselves-- believe in them for them.
If you have any respect for the bad actors, you'll acknowledge that they can & should seek their own therapy, self-help books, and financial resources etc to support self-growth.

It is that anxious, condescending, self-projecting streak that makes some sheep believe a wolf's own behavior *dooms* the wolf for all eternity, and that therefore the only humane response to bad behavior is empathy/forgiveness.

g) Sheep often don't absorb that communities actually *don't* have endless resources (time, attention, emotional bandwidth, care, etc) to pour into helping dysfunctional, harmful members figure out how not to be harmful.

And feedback for wolfish behavior can absolutely take the form of a fair, firm rejection from a community.

(To be clear, it's not a sheepdog's job to explain to a wolf nicely what he's doing & how to stop. If they can, it's always better tho, bc some wolves actually can change).

This is by necessity-- it'd be nice if shitty childhoods we weren't responsible for didn't become our problem to solve, but they just do. 

Otherwise, the community's waterline for acceptable behavior drops and we all suffer, and then our kids, too, will "just grow up like that."

I'd argue that wolves can actually grow and change with clear feedback, & sometimes this "empathy" is actually Enabler Logic-- "he doesn't *mean* to hit me, it's just how he grew up." 

Sure, and that's unfair. But it's on us to improve, if "how we grew up" is dysfunctional.

g) Sheep are often operating in a secretly fixed-mindset and condescending worldview.

They feel that a wolf who is wolfish due to bad social skills/trauma/confusion about boundaries/whatever understandable shit deserves pity, care, and understanding.

We sometimes don't like people for very good reasons-- we're intuiting personal characteristics in them that *will* lead to some kind of harm-- and this is valid, and not always just "fickle might of the popular kids" logic.

(Sheepdogs vary in discernment on this dimension).

We owe people a shot to surprise us, but if they consistently confirm a bad feeling inside, while that's important to query (as it ofc might be a projection of one's own trauma/bullshit), it's also important not to gaslight it.

This is tricky, and I'm going to say something controversial here-- I believe there actually is something valid and truthful a lot of the time in just not liking someone. Our intuitions know when something is off, esp seriously off.

f) That said, sheep also sometimes want the full justification to be laid out explicitly, and while this is a noble goal and is ideal, some instincts towards boundaries (in fact, often the best ones) exist in the realm of intuition.

They mix up fundamental rejection with conditional rejection, & think "if anyone can get fundamentally rejected w/o sufficient cause, I can too!" 

But a good sheepdog looks at a person's *behavior* to make the call, not just whether their soul seems worthy of saving, or whatever
d) how DIFFERENT they themselves are from the wolves-- anxious sheep will project their own fear of being considered fundamentally unworthy of belonging onto the wolves, & thus try to protect them

Sheep are also often blind to:

c) how wolves will use "the popular kids are bullying me" trope to give themselves more opportunities than they deserve (and end up causing more harm overall to a community than was necessary).

that is, making the most empathetic, fair choice you can for the good of all in a hard situation, a situation you didn't create, sometimes means somebody is gonna get hurt no matter what. 

When someone displays bad behavior & is unreachable on it, *somebody* will bear the cost.
But the best sheepdogs are already accounting for the unfortunate effects on the wolf in question, & are grappling deeply with the hard facts of leadership--

If there's gonna be a cost to the wolf, folks want to be sure it can't be avoided. Wanting reasons enumerated for kicking someone out etc is fair-- some sheepdogs are overly reactive, or are wolfish leaders themselves, posing as sheepdogs.
b) They're often blind to the fundamental costliness leadership decisions require.

a) the actual consequences of someone's bad behavior on the community. This includes everything from assault to consistently making the vibes worse at every social event.

I have a whitelist of trusted entities - you should too. Everything I see or hear I try and trace back to a trusted source. If you cannot trace it back, it is sus. Whitelist breaks manipulation attempts

The center of your trusted entities is you. Your firsthand knowledge. You know it's true because you see it, experience it. The second layer is people who give you information that you can verify is true for yourself. You don't trust experts, you test the experts
You should assume that anyone who feeds you any information will give you 10% completely false information. Either intentionally or unintentionally. Your goal is to find which 10% it is

Contrary to the pessimist's take: just because you're in a hostile information environment doesn't mean you have to verify everything yourself. You can trust people, take action on their information, and if it doesn't pan out, now you know

But overall, there's an issue with mathematization or modeling of biological systems, because they're far more chaotic than even economic ones.

This is why most people in complexity science almost have anything original. They simply use research and ideas developed in engineering, technology, medicine, physics, and even economics, and then frame them as complexity science.

Which means, in practice, you don't actually need to think in terms of complex systems much. You're still testing, adjusting, and learning empirically. So the idea of "complex systems" ends up being more of a framing than a useful method.

Since everything is a complex system, the concept becomes more philosophical than practical. You can't really control dynamic systems — at best, you make small changes and observe. But you can't predict the ultimate outcome, so you end up relying on experiments anyway.

What I want to convince you of is this isn't just a rule of court. It's a rule for life. Whenever you are suspicious that someone is not telling you the truth, one of the most powerful indicators that they are not is when they don't produce the evidence a truth-teller would.

That case puts it this way: "The production of weak evidence when strong is available can lead only to the conclusion that the strong would have been adverse." And it cites yet earlier cases that hold the same thing.

So CACI 203 states a legal rule that has been approved in California but is not unique to it. Indeed, courts apply this rule all over the country. Not only that, but it has blessed by the US Supreme Court in Interstate Circuit v. United States, from 1939.

We do this for 2 reasons. One is convenience: obviously, we don't want to spend precious time before trial writing instructions if we can help it. But two, pattern instructions are based on the language of case precedents and thus have already been approved by appellate courts.

So a quick background for non-lawyers-- pattern jury instructions are the manuals that we lawyers use that contain standard jury instructions for various types of cases. Rather than writing the jury instructions anew for  each case, we use instructions that have been compiled.

I want to do a quick thread about epistemology, featuring one of my favorite pattern jury instructions:  CACI 203.

"If a party provided weaker evidence when it could have provided stronger evidence, you may distrust the weaker evidence."

This is a rule to live your life by.

So, #ufotwitter, let's talk about some problems with the ETH hypothesis.

Here's an excellent example: Ron Sullivan, 1966, near Burke's Flat in Australia.

Guy is driving along, when some kind of "tractor beam" grabs his car. As it's pulling him, he sees his headlight beams *bend towards the side of the road*.

Now, here's the logical problem:

Light is what your eyes use to see.
This means that if the headlights are bending, then the light entering your eyes should *also* be bending along exactly the same path.
Literally any phenomenon that is bending light, is bending light. This is ... I mean, this is tautological.

Since your eyes use light to see, you won't see just the headlight beams bend.

You'll see the whole landscape sort of warp like a funhouse mirror.
If you don't see the whole landscape warp like a funhouse mirror, then *light isn't bending*; something else is going on.

when I take any kind of leadership role in a group, a significant fraction of the members inevitably project their daddy issues onto me, even people well into their 30s & 40s subconsciously demand I play a role in their story of the authoritian dad or the neglectful dad

the most satisfying groups have an abundance of adults fluidly negotiating who will lead in any given moment & domain

but that requires a level of maturity in group members, maybe even a rite of passage to comprehensively leave their childhood roles behind

the most painful groups I've had to deal with claim to have no hierarchy or centralised authority, while everyone pretends to not be engaged in a subterranean power struggle between multiple people with competing claims to being the ultimate authority

it's certainly possible to create a thriving group without relying on this hierarchical pattern, I've worked with 100s of them. but they require their members to transcend some of their earliest conditioning around power, authority, agency & conflict. which is a very big ask.

a group will often flow effortlessly well when there's 1 or 2 people holding an extra degree of responsibility (ie playing something like a mum/dad role). their authority can be very subtle and barely felt but subconsciously it provides a huge stabilising force in the group

no matter how enlightened or progressive your family, there's inevitably an enormous power difference between adults and children

this is the conditioning that basically everyone shows up with when they enter any collaboration

groups are tricky because we lack shared context, everyone comes from a different place, grew up with different norms and cultural expectations

but one thing nearly everyone has in common: you were probably raised in a household with 1 or 2 adults and a few kids
speaking as a specialist in non hierarchical organising, it is very confusing to discover in me a growing respect for hierarchy and understanding of the role it plays in nearly all groups of people
